articles.title: “How do I stop myself from choke slamming?”: Did Josh Jacobs really search controversial things on the internet amid domestic abuse trial?
articles.summary: NFL News: Josh Jacobs, the Green Bay Packers’ star player, has found himself in major legal trouble ahead of the new season as he faces two misdemeanor charges,.
articles.body: Josh Jacobs, the Green Bay Packers’ star player, has found himself in major legal trouble ahead of the new season as he faces two misdemeanor charges, battery and criminal damage to property, with his initial court appearance scheduled for November 17, 2026. Amid this, rumors about controversial searches on his phone have sparked chaos.Did Josh Jacobs search for controversial things about abuse amid his trial?No, Josh Jacobs' phone has not revealed any such thing. It has also not been confirmed if the Green Bay Packers’ star player’s phone was even checked.A few hours ago, a parody page on X made a post that read as, “𝗕𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗞𝗜𝗡𝗚: The prosecution in the Josh Jacobs assault trial says his phone revealed searches for: "Does the NFL really only fine you four games for abuse?” "How do I stop myself from choke slamming the people I love?" "How long is the movie Concussion?"”The post is completely made up but it has raised eyebrows among fans.A fan took to X and wrote, “Poor guy suffering from Postseason Depression.”Another fan joked, “I stand with Josh Jacobs. He just had postpartum depression.”A third fan posted, “I wouldn't mind a losing season. Kick his a*s off the team. Thank god he didn't introduce Trump. Phew”However, neither Josh Jacobs nor his legal team has reacted to the fake speculations yet.Will Josh Jacobs be allowed to play in the new season as his controversial trial sparks outrage in the league?The Green Bay Packers’ general manager Brian Gutekunst weighed in on the situation as he said, "We have not seen the video…Again, those are legal things going on right now, so we'll let those play out. That's really not for us, but in the appropriate times, if those things become available, we'll figure that stuff out when that time comes."NFL spokesperson Brian McCarthy said, "The matter remains under review of the personal conduct policy. We do not discuss details of an ongoing investigation."For now, it remains unconfirmed if Josh Jacobs will play in the new season as the Green Bay Packers coach Matt LaFleur said, There were many conversations obviously, and certainly don't know all the details. But what he tells me, I believe him and I trust him. I'm going to do that until proven otherwise."The Green Bay Packers’ general manager Brian Gutekunst added that fans might watch Josh Jacobs return to the field as he said, "I think that's to be seen, but I'm certainly hopeful that he will and certainly would expect that," Gutekunst said. "But we're going to let this process play out, and we'll be prepared either way."As per ESPN, Josh Jacobs will remain at the facility but it is not known if he will be allowed to take the field.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: What happens to Tony Romo's $72 million CBS deal now that he has officially pleaded no contest
articles.summary: NFL News: Tony Romo pleaded no contest Tuesday to an operating while intoxicated charge stemming from his July 23 arrest in Wisconsin. Milwaukee County court re.
articles.body: Tony Romo pleaded no contest Tuesday to an operating while intoxicated charge stemming from his July 23 arrest in Wisconsin. Milwaukee County court records show he lost his driving privileges for six months and was ordered to complete an alcohol assessment program. He also owes $834 in fines. In a statement posted to Instagram, Romo apologized and signaled his intent to return to CBS. The network had no comment. That silence is, arguably, the loudest thing CBS has said since this whole story began.Will Tony Romo return to CBS after his no-contest plea?Romo's statement was unambiguous about one thing. "The past month has been difficult, but it has also been personally significant," he wrote, adding that he intended to return to the broadcast booth. CBS, which issued a perfunctory one-line statement when it placed him on leave in July, offered nothing in response.That disconnect matters. Reporter John Ourand of Puck noted that Romo's statement was not coordinated with the network. That's not a minor procedural detail -- it signals a real split between the two sides. When a broadcaster and a network are on the same page, statements get aligned. They didn't here.CBS Sports president David Berson has maintained there is no timetable for a decision on Romo's future. J.J. Watt is already in the No. 1 seat alongside Jim Nantz and Tracy Wolfson. The Vikings-Packers opener on September 13 will be Watt's first real audition. That is not an accident.Can CBS terminate Tony Romo's contract over his OWI arrest?This is where the story gets genuinely complicated. Romo still has four years and roughly $72 million left on the 10-year, $180 million deal he signed in 2020. NFL insider Mike Florio wrote that if CBS tries to terminate his contract without paying out the remaining balance, it would likely set off what he called "a massive legal fight."Morals clauses in broadcasting contracts are typically written broadly. They can allow a network to argue that an employee's conduct damaged the organization's public image. But those clauses don't automatically give a network the right to walk away without cost. Romo's camp is already communicating with CBS about next steps, and his spokesperson made it clear he accepts full responsibility while framing the July arrest as an isolated civil matter. That framing is deliberate -- it's groundwork for any future legal argument.Florio added that if Romo's contract includes an arbitration clause, any dispute would likely stay out of open court. The most realistic outcome, he suggested, is a negotiated settlement, not a prolonged public battle. That makes sense. Neither side has much to gain from a courtroom fight that drags on through the NFL season.Is CBS already moving on from Tony Romo for good?Reading the situation honestly, the signs are not encouraging for Romo. CBS barred him from its NFL Media Day in New York. It did not include him in any of its Week 1 announcer pairings. Berson refused to offer any timetable for his return, and notably did nothing to push back on the perception that the network was done with him.Ourand reported that a return looks "exceedingly unlikely." That assessment tracks. The broader context also matters: Romo had already been drawing criticism for his on-air performances over the past few seasons, with many viewers openly preferring the work of Troy Aikman, Tom Brady, and Cris Collinsworth on rival networks. The arrest didn't create a problem at CBS -- it accelerated one that was already forming.Watt's performance over the first few weeks of the season will shape this more than any court filing. If he settles in comfortably, CBS will have every incentive to stop waiting on Romo and plenty of cover to do so. Romo still has a court date on September 21. Between now and then -- and likely well beyond it -- the $72 million question stays open.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Arch Manning, Jeremiah Smith and 2 more QBs in the top 10: 2027 NFL Draft big board entering Week 1
articles.summary: Why is Manning No. 1? His progression as a player was overlooked last year, but his play, along with his tools, indicated a future No. 1 draft pick. There's...
articles.body:
Week 1 of the NFL season is on the horizon and we're about to enter the REAL start of the college football season this weekend. But it's not too early to peek at the talent expected to hear their names called in the 2027 NFL Draft.

Here is my first big board, ranking players Nos. 1-31 and a list of 10 to watch who could break into the mix later this season. Why 31 instead of 30? You'll see why I gave both of those ranked players, each quarterbacks, some shine.

Manning is an excellent athlete with size. He plays with a proper timing on plays when working from the pocket, but he can also throw consistently on the move and has the toughness and core strength to get any throw off no matter his platform or how muddy the pocket is or how he is getting hit. He has a good arm that he unlocks because of his creativity, ability to anticipate and willingness to push the football down the field. Manning's quick throwing motion unlocks underneath throws and he already has advanced feel in the pocket. He constantly keeps his eyes downfield, which allows him to get the ball off and avoid sacks, turning negative plays to positive, or even explosive ones.

His progression as a player was overlooked last year after an early-season loss to Ohio State and Texas having to gut out several wins, but his play, along with his tools, indicated a future No. 1 draft pick despite what looked like lackluster performances. There's a lot of hype, but he looks like he's worth it.

A force of nature at receiver, Smith has been a standout player and absurdly productive at every level of his career. He is strong, explosive, and has an excellent build that allows him to bounce off tackles and constantly eat up yards after the catch. His power as a player makes him dangerous on in-breakers that allow him to build up speed and get downhill in a hurry, and his speed and burst out of breaks make him dangerous. Even without pristine route refinement, Smith is still dominant. It's hard to compare any athlete to Julio Jones, and welp, here we are with Smith. At worst you're looking at a Josh Gordon-like player.

A long athlete with range and advanced feel for the position, Moore affects a lot of throws with his length, and amplifies it with his body positioning. He has the speed to run with faster defenders, and the hand-eye coordination and timing to constantly make plays on the football. He showed those skills immediately as a true freshman starter in South Bend. Moore has a chance to be one of the best cornerback prospects I've ever studied.

A long, lean athlete with agility and gumby-like bend, Stewart can move around blocks in ways that few others can. He still needs refinement with how he uses his hands, but he has a wingspan like a pterodactyl to stave off blockers and flashes violent stabs and slaps that would unlock a whole new level with more consistency. Stewart's get-off and twitchiness make him dangerous off the edge or on games as either a penetrator or looper. He's what they look like.

Coleman would be looking like a definitive WR1 in any other class that doesn't feature Jeremiah Smith. Coleman is a tall outside receiver with long arms. His ball skills, catching range and hands are standout abilities that make him dangerous down the field and in the red zone. And when combined with his speed and twitch, it makes him an incredibly dangerous weapon. He's also a willing blocker, an appealing attribute for a receiver with such star qualities. Coleman hasn't been overwhelmingly productive in his career, which I attribute to the quarterbacks he played with and the simplistic route tree he was asked to run. Those are two things that should greatly improve this year in Austin. It's wild how much Coleman's build and game reminds me of A.J. Green.

A ridiculous runner and playmaker, it's Sellers' improvement as a passer, along with the blinding flashes of improvisational wizardry, that make him so exciting as a prospect. Sellers has a high-end arm that he can access from all platforms and is an excellent athlete with size at 6-foot-3, 238 pounds. He showed more consistency from the pocket in 2025, despite said pockets constantly being obliterated.

He didn't get a lot of help with his offensive surroundings at South Carolina, often having to pull a rabbit out of a hat just to throw the ball away because his protection broke down AND no one could get open. He is not a total wild horse, though; his decisions to scramble and improvise make sense. He will have the occasional spray, but I also think his calmer sense of play has led to improvements in accuracy, with an understanding of when to use touch on his throws. And he gets rid of the ball in a timely manner when the pocket is clean (and has shown a better understanding of when to throw the ball away).

It was notable that South Carolina offensive coordinator Mike Shula has put pre-snap operation on Sellers' plate on passing downs, a nice indicator of Sellers' handle of the offense. A new offensive coordinator in Kendal Briles and more competent personnel make me hopeful the results will look as good as Sellers' improved process has been. I am projecting a rise from Sellers this season and I'll be keen on revisiting Sellers around Halloween.

Moore is a calm operator whom Oregon asks to handle a lot mentally. He has good arm strength and is a good athlete who can throw consistently on the move. You can tell that Moore has really focused on his footwork and how to work through passing plays, and he constantly finds good answers to the problems defenses show him and tries to stay on time with the play.

There are times I wish Moore would push the ball a bit on high-low concepts, as he will too often defer to the "safer" of two options, especially when he feels pressure. I was encouraged with how he improved in this area in 2025 until some late season blemishes. I am keen to see how much more aggressive he is as a passer in 2026, which could help him really take a leap as a passer when the competition ramps up. Moore has also reportedly put on some bulk this offseason, and improved strength could help in tighter pockets with more bodies around him.

An easy mover with length and pop with his hands, Seaton's strong hands let him latch on and dominate defenders in the run game once he gets a hold of them. He still has work to do with his hand placement, eye awareness and technique, especially in pass protection, but Seaton has the twitch and size to be a valid blindside protector at the next level.

A massive, long left tackle, Goosby has light feet and can easily climb to the second level in the run game. Like most large offensive linemen, he can get caught playing high at times, but he is a good enough athlete to adjust as a pass protector. His length and agility allow him to recover against quicker pass rushers, and he has enough strength to get movement on double-teams. He still has things to clean up, but Goosby got much better as 2025 went along and should hopefully take another leap forward this year.

Simmons is an explosive athlete who is asked to do everything for Texas' defense. He is more of a front-seven weapon akin to Arvell Reese and Jalon Walker than a hand-in-the-dirt type, but Simmons can get after the passer with a quick first step and has the ability to run the hoop and turn a corner on offensive tackles. He gets asked to drop into coverage at a decent rate and also mirror athletic quarterbacks on passing downs, which is where he gets to show off his agility and speed.

I truly enjoyed watching Green play last year after his kick out to left tackle. He plays with excellent technique and awareness, his eyes are constantly going to the right spot against loopers and blitzers, and he is regularly firing off the football. He is a good overall athlete in a sturdy frame who plays with an advanced feel for the game (his ability to execute cutoff blocks in the run game is so fun to watch) and now Green has been a standout at both left guard and left tackle in his college career.

An outside receiver with size and long speed, Becker burst onto the scene in a talented wide receiver room last season at Indiana and was constantly coming down with big catches in big moments. Becker has strong hands and excellent hand-eye coordination in catching range that allows him to constantly come down with the football in contested-catch situations. He has long legs, but also shows enough quickness and bend to run a fully developed route tree, which pushes his ceiling up.

The other Texas offensive tackle prospect has a real chance of being the top offensive line prospect from this class when it's all said and done. Siani lined up at left tackle at Wake Forest and has the size, length and explosive athleticism to stay on the blindside, but he will line up on the right side this season in Austin. He is still cleaning up his hand usage and his pad level can get too high at times, but he has the freaky bend and light feet to recover whenever he gets out of position, and he brings some real pop when he connects in the run game, too. I might be getting over my skis with Siani, but I think he's going to keep ascending (he's relatively new to football) and be a real standout for Texas this year.

Stone is a disruptive defender who is asked to play all across the defensive line for Oklahoma. He'll play a chunk of snaps at nose tackle, but I think his best snaps are when he gets to play as a defensive end. Stone is strong, constantly keeps his feet upon contact, and can eat and split double-teams in the run game. His versatility works in his favor as his varied skill allows him to be a valid player at any spot.

It's not a shock that Green is a basketball player along with being a jumbo-sized tight end for LSU. He is built like a power forward, but fluid and quick enough as a route-runner and athlete that LSU would split him out and isolate him as a receiver. And he was constantly not only winning his route but creating yards after the catch as well. His size and ball skills also make him an obvious asset in the red zone.

Echoles is a uniquely built and powerful player who flashes quick hands to win early but stays active throughout the rep. He has good pop when engaging blockers and can anchor down in the run game. Echoles is young (turned 20 in August) and got better on an every-down basis as 2025 went along. He can stay on the field for all four downs and fill a variety of roles in a defense, with disruptive play and a unique combination of bulk, strength and quick feet.

Johnson has legit Y tight end size to hold up as a blocker in-line, and his strength shows up as a route-runner through contact. He is a good athlete who can consistently get in and out of his route breaks despite contact. And he can create a bit with the ball in his hands. He has the every-down skill set to excel at the next level.

Scott has good size to hold up in the middle but his value as a player comes with his disruption. He has a real ability to keep his feet while engaged on blocks while still attacking toward the football. Scott doesn't have a ton of production because of his interior alignment and the talent around him, but he still manages to affect the run and pass. If he starts finishing those plays and the game keeps slowing down for him, he should rise up the board. He's another young, talented defensive tackle in this class who got better as last year went along, especially during Miami's run to the national title game.

Robinson has the twitch, technique and foot quickness of a starting outside cornerback at the next level. He doesn't have top-end size (6-foot, 180 pounds) or strength. But he is a good athlete who has enough height and length to make plays on the football, with an ability to consistently track and play the football down the field. His awareness and burst lets him quickly recognize and close on underneath throws, too.

Washington can blow up double-teams with his size (listed 330 pounds) and strength. He has light feet and can get off the snap of the football to disrupt the offense as a pass rusher or to beat cutoff blockers. Washington can be used as a run down plugger, but can also fit on more attacking defenses that ask him to slant and twist after the snap. The fact that he can stay on the field as a pass rusher only adds to his appeal.

Baugh is a big back (6-foot-1, 225 pounds) but has the quickness and twitchiness of a much smaller athlete. He runs with balance and constantly does a nice job of setting up his blocks at the second level. Baugh doesn't have overwhelming long speed, but does have burst to get north in a hurry. He is a natural catcher of the football and has the size to hold up in pass protection as well, giving him every-down value. Just a cool player.

Johnson is a long and rangy athlete who can cover ground easily with his bouncy strides. He can play in the deep spot but Notre Dame rotates him down as a buzz defender to be near the box constantly. Johnson is willing to come down from depth to close in the run game and is an effective blitzer and overall tackler. Just watch last year's Pitt game to see what Johnson is capable of: he jumps a route for a pick 6, then follows it up on the next drive with a sack on a blitz and a tackle on the running back from depth. Johnson is an intriguing combination of athleticism, intelligence, and real football ability.

Hampton is a big and long corner who can play in zone and impact the game with his size and awareness, but might actually be most unlocked as a player in man coverage situations. He is not overly twitchy, but a smooth athlete who can fluidly get in and out of his turns. He reminds me a bit of James Bradberry IV.

Marsh has the size and fluidity as a route-runner to be a legit outside X wide receiver at the next level. He is able to bend as a route-runner and has a real feel for changing tempo and changing gears to keep cornerbacks uncomfortable. His feel on routes also shows up when he finds soft spots against zone. He doesn't have overwhelming speed, but he knows how to maximize it with his route-running, strong hands and ball skills. And that strength shows up with his blocking, which he's tenacious at, too. He should get a big boost in a better situation in Bloomington after transferring from Michigan State.

A transfer from Colorado, Miller has quick feet and the speed to threaten defenses vertically on every snap, as well as underneath throws and screens. Miller's fluid athleticism and ball skills are his standout traits as he can consistently flash late hands and not allow cornerbacks to get a read on when to play the football. He still has to add branches to his route tree, but Miller's ability to create explosive plays, hands and upside make him an exciting receiver prospect.

The former Legion of Boom coaches will drool over Jones, a tall (6-foot-4) and long outside cornerback who is constantly asked to work in-between, high-low concepts on the outside. Jones has real long speed to go with his size, too. He constantly is able to stay vertical with receivers and keep up with them on crossing routes. It's not all perfect, but just a little more refinement and Jones has an exciting combination of tools and real football ability.

Lutmer plays everywhere in the defensive backfield, from outside cornerback to, at times, even playing the box. His combination of speed, size, balance and twitchiness, along with his play strength, ability to read the game, and willingness to tackle make him a valid prospect at cornerback, slot or safety.

Traore plays with strong hands and can affect the run and pass with his ability to strike and push the pocket. He isn't the longest player, but he knows how to use the length he has and his combination of burst and aggressiveness make him a tough player to block. There's some Jared Verse to his game.

Brown is a very good athlete who can work sideline-to-sideline in the run game or in coverage and get downhill in a hurry as a blitzer (where he flashes some bend around the edge, too). He is better in space right now than he is working through the muck and getting off blocks, but his combination of size, speed (he seriously runs like a deer), and aggressiveness will allow his game to translate nicely to the NFL.

I consider the next two quarterbacks right next to each other. Both are big, toolsy prospects and both have a feel for ball placement and for playing the position (and both might be better served as candidates for the 2028 draft).

Lindsey is the classic quarterback archetype of the big-armed pocket passer in the vein of Drew Bledsoe. Listed at 6-foot-5, 230 pounds, Lindsey is willing and able to stand and deliver the football in the (constantly) muddy pockets he has to deal with behind Minnesota's offensive line. Despite his size, he has a quick delivery, is a solid athlete, and has clean footwork to throw on the move or after turning his back to the defense (he has a good amount of reps already from under center). He's still young as a redshirt sophomore, so he might still be a year away, but Lindsey is definitely one to keep an eye on as a potential riser.

Much will be made about Mestemaker's lack of experience as a starting quarterback at any level (he was a backup in high school and a walk-on at North Texas), but despite not having the experience or snaps that other typically highly touted quarterbacks have, he just seems to know how to play the position. He has a good arm that can access all parts of the field and is willing to push the ball from muddy pockets. He can change arm slots and layer the football up and over defenders when needed. Mestemaker is tall (6-foot-3) and has a long frame that he can continue to fill out (my biggest area for improvement with him would be play strength to withstand knocks in the pocket). But he is athletic, has a loose arm, and is willing to move and work from the pocket and has enough giddy-up to work outside it, too. I'm excited to watch Mestemaker continue to progress this year at Oklahoma State.

articles.title: Updated Fantasy Football Rankings After the 2026 Preseason
articles.summary: One week. That's all that stands between us and the first game of the 2026 NFL season. When the Seattle Seahawks and New England Patriots kick off their Super Bowl LX rematch on Sept. 9, another fantasy football season will begin.
articles.body:
One week. That's all that stands between us and the first game of the 2026 NFL season. When the Seattle Seahawks and New England Patriots kick off their Super Bowl LX rematch on Sept. 9, another fantasy football season will begin.

That leaves one final draft weekend: One last chance for managers who have been drafting all summer, and the first opportunity for those who have waited until the last minute to assemble a roster for the season ahead.

The end of draft season is always exciting, nerve-wracking and a little sad.

We're here to build on that excitement, ease those nerves and dry those tears. You'll find a range of resources to help make your final draft of 2026 your best, including PPR rankings by position and overall, plus values and sleepers to target and busts to avoid.

Before we get to the position-by-position rankings, let's take a look at the draft-day landscape from 10,000 feet with a list of the top fantasy players overall in PPR leagues in 2026.

As we do, though, consider this piece of wisdom from the great philosopher Michael Gerard Tyson: "Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the mouth."

Follow this list blindly and take the highest-ranked player in every round, and you could run into trouble. Likewise, rigidly committing to a Zero RB approach without accounting for how the draft is unfolding can leave you at a disadvantage.

Stay alert: Draft flow and the approaches of other managers can significantly affect your decisions. Preparation is essential, but you must remain flexible when the draft does not unfold as expected.

Be ready, be flexible and remember the one principle that should guide you: value.

Quarterback is the most important position in the NFL. But that importance doesn't carry over into fantasy football.

This isn't to say elite signal-callers don't have value. But that value is muted by the high price tag it takes to acquire them in drafts. More often than not, the "edge" gained by drafting a high-end QB isn't worth the hole it leaves at running back or wide receiver.

The smart play at quarterback is patience. There are signal-callers available in the QB8-QB12 range with legitimate top-five upside, and you can be the last team in a 12-team league to draft a starter under center and still be fine.

Trevor Lawrence, Jacksonville Jaguars ( ADP : QB10)

Lawrence finished last year fourth among quarterbacks in fantasy points, and from Week 10 on he quietly led the position. The Jaguars have no shortage of passing-game weapons and Liam Coen's offense has produced back-to-back top-five finishes at quarterback. Three in a row is a real possibility.

Nix has shown no ill effects from the fractured ankle that ended his 2025 season. The Broncos added a high-end weapon in the offseason in wide receiver Jaylen Waddle, and Denver was quietly fourth in the league last year with 613 pass attempts. Nix was seventh in fantasy points among quarterbacks a year ago.

Allen is an example of why high-end fantasy quarterbacks aren't worth the high-end price tag. Yes, he was fantasy's highest scoring quarterback last year, but it was by less than a fantasy point per game over Matthew Stafford, who came off the board over 10 rounds later.

Joe Burrow, Cincinnati Bengals (ADP: QB3)

Burrow is the highest-ranked pure pocket passer in terms of average draft position—and that is not a good thing. For him to return value, he has to post ridiculous passing numbers a la two years ago. He also has a lengthy history and plays behind a sketchy offensive line.

Goff isn't an especially exciting fantasy option. He doesn't have any rushing upside. But he was second in the league in passing yards last year, is at the helm of one of the NFL's most prolific offenses and he hasn't finished lower than seventh in fantasy points among quarterbacks over the past three years.

Kyler Murray, Minnesota Vikings (ADP: QB17)

Murray won the starting job under center in the Twin Cities. The Vikings offense has plenty of weapons. Murray has demonstrated elite fantasy upside in the past. And we have already seen Kevin O'Connell have success with a reclamation project.

Whether you're an old-school fantasy drafter who likes to attack the running back position early or a Zero RB drafter who prefers to fade the position until the later rounds, there's one buzzword to remember where running backs are concerned: scarcity.

Running back is the shallowest position in fantasy football. In an era of committee attacks and muddied backfields, the number of every-down workhorses seemingly shrinks by the year.

Never mind the injuries that have already hit the position this year. Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty and Arizona Cardinals running back Jeremiyah Love are already dealing with ankle injuries, with Love reportedly sidelined by a high ankle sprain. Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs is on the Commissioner's Exempt List following an offseason arrest.

Proceed with caution: the backfield is full of potential pitfalls.

Kyren Williams, Los Angeles Rams (ADP: RB15)

Yes, Williams ceded some touches to Blake Corum over the second half of last season. But his efficiency numbers were better than in 2024, and his yardage and fantasy production remained essentially unchanged. Williams is going to post a fourth straight top-10 fantasy campaign—with an RB2 price tag in drafts.

Tony Pollard, Tennessee Titans (ADP: RB30)

Pollard inspires little enthusiasm among fantasy drafters, but he's the unquestioned lead back for the Titans. Pollard and Derrick Henry of the Baltimore Ravens are the only two active running backs with four straight 1,000-yard seasons on the ground.

Christian McCaffrey, San Francisco 49ers (ADP: RB3)

McCaffrey was fantasy's highest-scoring running back last year, but there's zero chance he repeats that feat. He is a 30-year-old running back coming off a career-high 413 touches who missed 13 games both times he has come off a season with 2,000 total yards in his career.

Jeremiyah Love, Arizona Cardinals (ADP: RB13)

This analyst was already avoiding Love at his ADP because of concerns about the Cardinals' offense. Now, the third overall pick in April's draft enters his first professional season managing an ankle injury. With Tyler Allgeier also on the roster and $54 million in guaranteed money committed to their rookie runner, Arizona has ample reason to manage his workload carefully early in the season.

Chuba Hubbard, Carolina Panthers (ADP: RB36)

With Hubbard missing a chunk of camp and all of the preseason with a bad hamstring, many fantasy managers have anointed Jonathon Brooks the lead back in Carolina and written Hubbard off entirely. But Brooks has carried the ball all of nine time for 22 yards over two seasons in the NFL. He's also torn his ACL twice.

Chris Rodriguez Jr., Jacksonville Jaguars (ADP : RB43)

The general consensus among fantasy managers is that Bhayshul Tuten is the running back to roster in fantasy leagues this year. But Rodriguez is a Liam Coen favorite who has averaged 4.6 yards per carry in his career. The backfield workload in Duval County could wind up being a lot closer to an even split.

The days of wide receivers as second-class citizens in fantasy football are over.

With more and more teams running pass-heavy schemes and sets with three or four wide receivers, the list of fantasy-relevant wideouts has grown.

Add in the prevalence of PPR scoring, and elite wideouts can throw down just as many points as their counterparts at running back. As a whole, wide receivers also have a lower bust rate.

Given those realities, many fantasy managers now swear by addressing the position early and often. But wide receiver is considerably deeper than running back. Once you get beyond the top 36 RBs, the drop-off becomes much steeper. At that point in the wide receiver rankings, though, there are still plenty of players who can help a fantasy team.

No position affords more flexibility than wide receiver. Take advantage of it.

Jaylen Waddle, Denver Broncos (ADP: WR20)

Waddle is one of this analyst's favorite wide receiver targets. He has demonstrated top-10 upside in the past and appears to have developed a quick rapport with quarterback Bo Nix. Waddle projects to be the Broncos' No. 1 receiver in 2026 and should outperform this draft cost by a wide margin.

Carnell Tate, Tennessee Titans (ADP: WR32)

It's understandable that fantasy mangers have some concerns about the passing attack in Tennessee after the team was 30th in the league in that regard a year ago. But Cam Ward showed an affinity for chucking the rock downfield as a rookie, and in 2026 those vertical targets are going to go to the fourth overall pick in April's draft.

Malik Nabers, New York Giants (ADP: WR12)

The fantasy ceiling with Nabers is sky-high—he was sixth in PPR points among wide receivers as a rookie. But while it looks like he will be a go for Week 1 after tearing his ACL last season, the lack of an offseason isn't going to help his chances of a fast start. He is being drafted far closer to his fantasy ceiling than his floor.

Rashee Rice, Kansas City Chiefs (ADP: WR13)

On a per-game basis, Rice has demonstrated elite fantasy upside. But he's also had all kinds of trouble staying in those games—he has missed an average of 11 games a season the past two years. Throw in Patrick Mahomes returning from an ACL tear, and Rice is a pass as a high-end fantasy WR2.

Stefon Diggs, Washington Commanders (ADP: WR41)

Diggs was quietly good for the New England Patriots and fantasy managers alike last year, catching 85 passes, topping 1,000 receiving yards and finishing inside the top-20 wide receivers in PPR points. Expecting a repeat is pushing the boundaries of optimism, but expecting cheap WR3 numbers isn't.

Jalen Coker, Carolina Panthers (ADP: WR54)

Coker's numbers over his first two seasons have been relatively modest, but the Panthers thought enough of him to offer a lucrative offseason extension. Carolina head coach Dave Canales has identified him as the team's No. 2 receiver. If Bryce Young takes a step forward in 2026, Coker could be one of the biggest beneficiaries.

Drafting a tight end in 2026 is like playing Let's Make a Deal : There are three doors to choose from. Fantasy managers just need to hope they find the Big Deal—and avoid getting zonked.

Door No. 1 is the elite options. They have a high ceiling, a relatively high floor and a high price tag to go along with it.

Door No. 2 is the Tier 2 tight ends—a handful of TEs who have the potential to crack the top tier but also face question marks. Lower prices. Higher risk.

Then there's Door No. 3: the late-round options outside the top 10. The upside is that if one of these tight ends hits, you can find excellent value. The downside is the uncertainty—drafting two may be prudent because none is a sure thing.

This analyst appears to be choosing Door No. 3 more often than not in 2026—and isn't sure that's a good idea.

Travis Kelce, Kansas City Chiefs (ADP: TE11)

Yes, Kelce is 73 years old. Or 36. Whatever. Yes, Kelce averaged a career-low 50.1 receiving yards per game in 2025. But even in that "down" season, he finished third among tight ends in PPR scoring. The last time Kelce did not finish as a top-five fantasy tight end was 2014.

Isaiah Likely, New York Giants (ADP: TE12)

After four years in Mark Andrews' shadow in Baltimore, Likely followed John Harbaugh to New York. When the targets were there for him with the Ravens, he showed legitimate top-five fantasy upside. And with Malik Nabers sitting much of the summer, Likely has had all sorts of time to build a connection with Jaxson Dart.

Trey McBride, Arizona Cardinals (ADP: TE2)

This isn't to say McBride shouldn't be the second tight end drafted. But as we have moved through the summer, all the value has been drained from his asking price—he's being drafted just a few spots after Brock Bowers now. McBride is going to regress after a historic 2025 campaign. The only question is by how much.

Harold Fannin Jr., Cleveland Browns (ADP: TE8)

Fannin had an outstanding rookie season, leading the Browns in receptions, receiving yards and touchdown catches while finishing sixth among tight ends in PPR scoring. However, Cleveland's offensive uncertainty is one of several factors that could make a repeat performance difficult.

Juwan Johnson, New Orleans Saints (ADP: TE16)

Johnson is generating little in the way of fantasy buzz this summer, but he quietly ranked inside the top five among tight ends in both receptions and receiving yards last year on the way to a ninth-place finish in fantasy points. With Jordyn Tyson out indefinitely, Johnson should see a robust target share early in the season.

TE Greg Dulcich, Miami Dolphins (ADP: TE26)

To be clear, Dulcich isn't an elite talent—he's never had even 425 receiving yards in a season. But someone is going to have to catch the ball in Miami this year, and he had a strong camp. This is a dart throw, but it could pay off if Dulcich starts piling up garbage-time stats.

Despite all protestations and proclamations that swear there is, there really isn't a "best" draft strategy.

Leagues can be won and lost in all sorts of ways. Fantasy managers need to choose a plan they are comfortable executing—and be ready to pivot when another manager disrupts it three rounds into the draft.

That's fantasy football. Flexibility is critical on draft day. Except where defenses and kickers are involved. There, the strategy is rigid: wait.

In the vast majority of fantasy leagues, there is no reason to draft a defense and a kicker before your final two picks—in that order.

For a defense, target a unit with one or two favorable early matchups. When the schedule becomes less favorable, turn to the waiver wire. For a kicker, take the best option available.

Jacksonville Jaguars Defense (ADP: DST10)

Again, the smart play with defenses is to target a good one with a plus matchup or two to open the season. The schedule admittedly stiffens for the Jaguars after the opener, but the NFL's No. 1 run defense from a year ago hosts a Browns team that fielded the league's second-worst scoring offense in 2025.

Cam Little, Jacksonville Jaguars (ADP: PK5)

There is no reason why Little shouldn't be the first kicker drafted, if only because it's just a joy to have the youngster on a fantasy roster. There's a lot to be said for the feeling you get when he lines up for a 62-yard attempt and you know he's going to punch it through halfway up the uprights.

Aaron Donald's return gives the Rams an even more formidable front after the team added edge rusher Myles Garrett and cornerback Trent McDuffie. Expectations for Los Angeles' defense are understandably high. However, its early schedule is challenging, with four 2025 playoff teams among its first five opponents.

Brandon Aubrey, Dallas Cowboys (ADP: PK1)

Aubrey is a fantastic kicker—he's been a Pro Bowler all three years in the NFL and never finished lower than third in fantasy points among kickers. But even in his first-place season at the position (2023), he outscored the 10th-ranked kicker by less than two points per game. There's no edge there. Just a wasted flier.

The Raiders defense was not especially good last season—to put it kindly. However, Las Vegas invested heavily in its front seven during free agency and retained edge rusher Maxx Crosby. More importantly for early-season streaming, the Raiders open against a Dolphins offense with significant questions entering 2026.

Chris Boswell, Pittsburgh Steelers (ADP: PK13)

Boswell is not the flashiest fantasy option, but he has been productive. As recently as 2024, no kicker scored more fantasy points. He also plays for an offense that should be competent, if not elite—the type of unit that can stall in the red zone and create frequent field-goal opportunities.

Gary Davenport is a two-time Fantasy Sports Writers Association Football Writer of the Year. Follow Gary on X at @IDPGodfather .

articles.title: Every Division's 'Wild Card' for the 2026 NFL Season
articles.summary: Every NFL division has "that team."
articles.body:
You know the one: They could get hot and make a playoff run, but they could just as easily suffer a season-long meltdown resulting in a premium first-round pick.

The gap between the ceiling and floor is particularly large, often because of unknowns at quarterback, within the coaching staff, or throughout the core of the roster.

These are the teams that might play spoiler, but could just as easily see their own seasons spoiled well before Halloween.

The Ceiling: New Dolphins head coach/former Packers defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley could immediately get into a groove with 27-year-old former third-round pick Malik Willis, who generated nine passing/rushing touchdowns to zero interceptions and posted a 134.6 passer rating in limited action the last two years in Green Bay. The result could be a competitive season and a wild-card opportunity for Miami.

The Floor: Saddled with arguably the least-talented pass-catching group in the NFL and stuck behind an offensive line riddled with question marks, Willis struggles mightily in his first sustained run as a starter as a rebuilding team hits rock bottom.

Spoiler Factor: Even with everything falling apart the last couple years, they've played the Bills tough. In their last three meetings, they're 1-2 with a plus-four scoring margin.

The Ceiling: This season could be to Deshaun Watson what 2010 was to Michael Vick. Vick had been a non-factor for several seasons in a row before winning Comeback Player of the Year in an oft-dominant age-30 campaign with the Eagles. The 30-year-old Watson certainly has the talent and finds himself in that spot now. He's surrounded by intriguing young talent, a revamped offensive line and a new-look coaching staff. Those are the ingredients for a surprisingly competitive season.

The Floor: Watson could just as easily fall on his face again, and that young offensive supporting cast may need time to grow in a new system. There are no guarantees with the line, and the defense will almost certainly struggle sans Myles Garrett. They could easily end up with the No. 1 overall pick.

Spoiler Factor: In the second half last season, they went 2-1 with a positive scoring margin within the division. They've generally played Baltimore, Pittsburgh and Cincinnati tough in recent years.

The Ceiling: They get a full season from the Daniel Jones who posted a 109.9 passer rating during a 7-1 start to the 2025 season. That and strong contributions from Jonathan Taylor, an underrated and talented receiving corps and an experienced offensive line could carry them to a division title.

The Floor: They get the version of Daniel Jones who posted an 84.2 passer rating as the team went 1-4 following that hot start—a stretch that ended with him tearing his right Achilles. If he cannot stay healthy, Indianapolis could get even less. Combined with an overall lack of oomph on either side of the ball, that could leave the Colts fighting the Titans for third place in the division.

Honorable Mention in the Division: Speaking of the Titans, they were a respectable 2-3 from the start of December onward last season as top pick Cam Ward put up six touchdowns to zero interceptions and posted a 103.8 passer rating in his final four starts as a rookie. Could a new coaching staff maintain that trajectory? Or is this still a full-on rebuild that will require at least another roller-coaster of a season?

The Ceiling: We've seen it. It remains Super Bowl-high so long as Patrick Mahomes and Andy Reid are cooking.

The Floor: We got a glimpse in 2025. If a 30-year-old Mahomes can't stay healthy and regain some of the magic from his 20s despite a significantly weaker supporting cast, the Chiefs will have an extremely difficult time hanging with the Broncos and Chargers.

Honorable Mention in the Division: There's no denying that the Raiders, who have invested considerable draft capital the last few offseasons and spent huge in free agency this spring, have plenty of talent in key spots. If they could catch fire with Kirk Cousins or Fernando Mendoza, they could remarkably send the Chiefs to the AFC West basement and hang with the Broncos and Chargers. Or it could be a total mess as the rebuild trudges on.

The Ceiling: There's a world in which Jaxson Dart takes off in his second season and becomes a star with top-notch support from an exciting skill-position group, a promising offensive line, a defense that features massive talent up front and an incoming head coach with Super Bowl pedigree. In that world, the Giants can shock the unpredictable NFC East.

The Floor: Ultimately, it remains low with so many questionable variables. The sample is small for Dart, and two key cogs (Malik Nabers and Cam Skattebo) are coming back from major injuries. If the Eagles are the Eagles, a better defense helps Dallas bounce back, and Washington can rediscover what got it to the NFC title game in 2024, the Giants could be in for a third consecutive last-place campaign.

Spoiler Factor: At home in 2025, the Giants beat the Eagles and Cowboys by a combined margin of 68-34.

The Ceiling: They won 14 games in 2024. The core remains similar, but with wild-card Kyler Murray at quarterback. If Murray can stay healthy and produce to his talent level, the sky (or a surprise NFC North crown) is the limit for a team with a superstar receiver, a stacked offensive line and a high-quality defense.

The Floor: Murray reproduces the uneven form he showed over his final four seasons in Arizona, missing at least six games in three campaigns and posting a mediocre 90.3 passer rating overall. If a new environment cannot reignite the former No. 1 overall pick and J.J. McCarthy cannot provide a viable alternative, Minnesota is a .500-ish team at best.

Spoiler Factor: The Vikings finished the 2025 season on a five-game winning streak despite issues at quarterback. That run included multi-score victories over division rivals Detroit and Green Bay, as the team went 4-2 against the NFC North for the second consecutive season.

The Ceiling: If Tua Tagovailoa or Michael Penix Jr. can deliver, the Falcons could prevail in the wide-open NFC South behind Bijan Robinson, who is in his prime, a fresh coaching staff, a solid offensive line and a budding defense.

The Floor: Tagovailoa may have peaked several years ago, while Penix may have peaked in the Pac-12. If so, there's only so much Robinson and a decent skill-position corps can do for a team that will likely still struggle defensively as well. They can wind up with seven or eight wins for a sixth season in a row.

Honorable Mention in the Division: Tyler Shough had a triple-digit passer rating in the final four weeks of his rookie season for a Saints squad that finished 4-1. That momentum and a sneaky-solid offseason could take New Orleans back to the top of the division. However, they're less than a sophomore slump away from a return to the basement.

The Ceiling: A similar 49ers core lost the Super Bowl by a field goal a few years ago, so San Francisco's ceiling entering 2026 is clearly championship level. Imagine what this experienced, well-coached and deeply talented team could accomplish if it simply stays healthy.

The Floor: Another injury-plagued campaign likely means another third-place finish when you're dealing with the Super Bowl favorite (Los Angeles) and the defending Super Bowl champion (Seattle).

Spoiler Factor: They beat both the Rams and Seahawks on the road in 2025. In fact, they haven't lost a regular-season game in Seattle since 2021.

articles.title: Three Things Texas QB Arch Manning Must Prove Before The 2027 NFL Draft
articles.summary: Arch Manning is aiming to become the third member of his family to be the No. 1 pick in the NFL Draft. Here's how he can solidify that spot.
articles.body: Texas quarterback Arch Manning enters his redshirt junior season as the most celebrated and scrutinized quarterback in the country and thus is the most intriguing NFL prospect. But he's not a shoo-in to be the No. 1 overall pick of the 2027 NFL Draft. There is no denying Manning’s appeal. He’s supremely talented, boasting an ideal blend of size, arm talent and mobility with the Hall of Fame bloodlines every QB-needy NFL franchise would seemingly love to build its team around. But is it as simple as Manning, whose 2026 season kicks off Saturday against Texas State, "just staying healthy" before earning the distinction of being the top pick next spring? To put it bluntly, no. In a class this gifted, no one can afford to simply rest on their résumé. Not Manning nor Ohio State phenom receiver Jeremiah Smith nor any of the top QBs. But, if Manning can improve in three particular areas, I believe he will follow in his famous uncles’ footsteps and hear his name called first on draft day. 1. Improve In The Quick Game Like most quarterbacks drawing attention from NFL scouts, Manning will ultimately get drafted because of his ability to accurately throw the football long distances. It is easy to assume that if a quarterback is accurate on longer passes, he’ll also be precise on shorter throws. That was not the case with Manning last year, however. In fact, he was arguably at his worst on the shortest throws — a flaw that simply must be corrected if he is to earn an early first-round selection next spring. The so-called quick game — i.e. slants, bubble screens, pop passes — is as fundamental to the modern era of football as shooting 3-pointers is to modern basketball. These routes have gained importance in recent years with today’s elite pass-rushers and all the exotic scheming and blitzing done to pressure quarterbacks immediately. Signal-callers absolutely must be able to get the ball in and out of their hands efficiently. When operating out of the shotgun — as Manning typically did in 2025 — quarterbacks are taught to first secure the snap and then simultaneously turn their feet in the direction of the intended receiver while spinning the ball to allow their fingers to grip the laces. Once the ball is comfortably in their grasp, a quick, strong throw should be out long before the pass rush has any chance to get home. Experienced quarterbacks can make these throws seem like little more than extended handoffs, collecting and distributing in one fluid motion. Manning is as quick as you’ll see in this regard. In fact, he’s quicker than most. However, his technique was off and therefore so was his accuracy. Manning didn’t consistently pair his upper and lower body last season, failing to either grip the laces or turn his feet properly (or both), resulting in the ball spraying erratically. These issues were further exacerbated by a sloppy sidearm release that left potential pass-catchers struggling to pick up the ball in flight. With less distance for the ball to cover, receivers had a hard time locating and corralling throws that came in at the head or knee level just as often as they did near the chest, as intended. Manning’s inconsistent accuracy forced receivers to adjust, contributing to a whopping 22 charted drops by Texas receivers, per PFF. It also disrupted opportunities to create yards after the catch. Fortunately, this is a coachable skill that a lot of young quarterbacks struggle with. Manning did improve in this area over the course of last season, eventually showing both greater poise and precision. I expect he will be even better in his second year as the Longhorns’ starter. 2. Work Through His Progressions Better Too often last year, Manning stared down his primary target and either tried to throw him open or resorted to scrambling. While he was fairly successful at improvising, the competition will be much better in the NFL. It is difficult to convey Manning’s struggles in this area with statistics, but consider this: Per Pro Football Focus, Manning had 10 passes batted down at the line of scrimmage last year. Of all the quarterbacks selected in the NFL Draft in April, only fellow first-year starter Ty Simpson had this many throws knocked down — and that's with the 6-foot-1 Simpson attempting 69 more passes at Alabama last year than the 6-foot-4 Manning did for Texas. It is the same story if we compare Manning to the rest of this year’s loaded quarterback class. There were four other quarterbacks to make the first round in my way-too-early 2027 mock draft from April, and none of them cracked double-digits in this category. The same goes for Notre Dame’s CJ Carr (four), Miami’s Darian Mensah (seven) and Oklahoma State’s Drew Mestemaker (eight), who are also receiving first-round buzz heading into this season. Now, just as Manning's receivers deserve some of the criticism for the aforementioned drops, at least partial blame for batted down passes belongs to his blockers. But Manning greatly contributed to these deflections at the line of scrimmage by too often telegraphing his throws. This allowed rushers to time their leaps and, sometimes, tip his passes for their teammates to potentially intercept. Part of Manning’s appeal to NFL teams is his prototypical height and lightning-quick release. Frankly, there is only one excuse for a quarterback of Manning’s size and arm talent to have this many passes knocked down in Steve Sarkisian’s shotgun-based offense, and that is inexperience. NFL teams will forgive Manning’s "rookie mistakes" if they were, indeed, just that. But to be the No. 1 overall pick next spring, Manning must prove he can scan the entire field, efficiently moving from his primary target to second or third options while protecting the ball. 3. Just Win, Baby (Including On The Road) Fans would be amazed at how much value NFL teams place on wins as a starting QB. It isn’t that professional scouts fail to recognize the impact that a leaky defense, turnovers by others or a porous offensive line might play in determining the outcome of a game. They know that football is the ultimate team sport and, while quarterback is the most important position on the field, he’s still just one of 22 players in a given play. But a QB meriting strong consideration for a first-round pick — especially No. 1 overall — must demonstrate the ability to uplift his teammates. Never mind the Heisman hype; he simply needs to be great when the lights shine brightest. Manning will surely be under that spotlight (and microscope) while trying to lead a Texas program to its first national title in 21 years. A lot of Fernando Mendoza’s skeptics quieted down last year once he guided the Indiana Hoosiers past Ohio State in the Big Ten title game, much less past Alabama, Oregon (for a second time) and Miami in the College Football Playoff. Mendoza completed 70.0% of his passes with 10 touchdowns against just two interceptions in those five games. For the year, he completed 72.0% of his throws with 41 touchdowns against six interceptions. In other words, his performance was largely the same all year long, regardless of opponent. Now contrast that with Manning, who was picked off in all three of Texas’ losses last year and completed 58.8% of his passes against Oregon, Florida and Georgia with a 4:4 touchdown-to-interception ratio. (It is worth noting that each of those losses came on the road.) He threw 22 touchdowns with just three interceptions while completing 62.2% of his passes in his 10 other starts. Manning won’t have many opportunities this fall to slay any perceived road demons, at least not during the regular season, making his performance in a select few contests that much more important. Only three games on the Longhorns' schedule — at Tennessee, at Missouri and at LSU — are outside the state of Texas. That's not to say UT's schedule will be comfortable, however. Matchups against fellow preseason top-10 teams such as Ohio State, Oklahoma, Texas A&M and Ole Miss are sure to challenge Manning and Co. How he responds will not only define the 2026 Longhorns but very likely the top of the 2027 NFL Draft.

articles.title: “There’s still parts of my brain I’m trying to rewire”: Puka Nacua’s ex GF Hallie Aiono opens up about psychiatrist visit after four-year relationship and alleged abuse
articles.summary: NFL News: It’s not easy to open up about loving someone for four years – the kind of love you felt in your bones. It’s not easy to publicly admit that the perso.
articles.body: It’s not easy to open up about loving someone for four years – the kind of love you felt in your bones. It’s not easy to publicly admit that the person you once loved made you feel extreme betrayal, abuse, and neglect, leaving you feeling crushed and as though your brain chemistry had been altered.It’s not easy to meet with a psychiatrist and revisit some of the darkest days of your life.It’s not easy to share a child with someone you believe caused so much pain and then still hope for a normal life, a healthy love, and a brighter future with an open heart and an open mind after everything you have been through.But Puka Nacua’s ex-girlfriend, Hallie Aiono, is trying. Trying with all her might -for herself, for her son Kingston, and for the future she hopes to build for her future children.Puka Nacua’s ex-girlfriend Hallie Aiono opens up about her psychiatrist visit and mental health journeyOpening up about mental health is rarely easy, particularly when the experiences behind those struggles are profoundly personal. Hallie Aiono, the former girlfriend of Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua, has shared a candid update about her decision to meet with a psychiatrist.Aiono, who shares a son, Kingston, with Nacua, said she has spent the past year and a half working through some of the most difficult experiences of her life.She revealed that she would soon be meeting with a psychiatrist, admitting that discussing mental health publicly makes her uncomfortable.For years, Aiono feared receiving a mental health “label,” believing that asking for help meant she was weak or that something was wrong with her. Her perspective, however, has gradually changed.Aiono explained that she has experienced anxiety for as long as she can remember and has also gone through periods of depression. She expressed curiosity about whether ADHD [Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder] or OCD [Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder] could help explain some of the ways her mind works.Above all, Aiono said she wants to understand herself better and become “the healthiest version” of herself.However, her willingness to discuss intensely personal struggles is not entirely new. During her pregnancy, Aiono previously shared candid posts about body dysmorphia and her changing relationship with her appearance [3 months pregnancy look compared to 9 months pregnancy look].Hallie Aiono reflects on four-year relationship and alleged abuseThe most emotional part of Aiono’s message centered on a previous four-year relationship [supposedly with Puka Nacua] and the drastic change she experienced after loving someone completely.Aiono alleged that she went from feeling intensely connected to her former partner to experiencing “extreme betrayal, abuse” and “complete neglect.” While some portions of her personal life became public, she said the experiences that happened away from public view [probably behind closed doors] affected her most profoundly.She said those experiences “completely crushed” her and left her feeling as though her brain chemistry had been altered.Although Aiono said she has made significant progress over the past year and a half, she admitted some of the emotional effects remain, and she still needs to rewire them.“Right now, I’m just really trying to understand myself,” Aiono said in the TikTok video.“Understand why my brain works the way it works. Why I react the way I react. I’m just trying to find the healthiest version of myself, especially after the past year and a half.”She added, “I’ve talked about it on here a few other times, but I have experienced the darkest, darkest days of my life in the past year and a half, and I have healed so much. I really have. But I also feel like there’s still parts of my brain that I’m trying to rewire.”These are Aiono’s allegations and descriptions of her own experiences. She has previously made public accusations and shared critical posts regarding Nacua during her pregnancy and amid their highly publicized personal and legal disputes. She reportedly labeled him a “narcissist,” too.Puka Nacua’s ex Hallie Aiono wants a healthier future for her son KingstonFor Aiono, meeting with a psychiatrist appears to be about more than finding answers about anxiety or depression. She said she wants to better understand herself and learn how to move forward without letting past experiences dictate what she believes love should look or feel like.Motherhood is also a crucial part of her motivation. Aiono said she wants to become the best version of herself for Kingston and for any future children she may have.By speaking openly about her fears surrounding psychiatric care, Aiono turned a profoundly personal moment into a powerful message for others who may also feel afraid to seek help: asking for support is not a sign of weakness.For Aiono, taking that first step appears to be part of the healthier future she says she wants to build - both for herself and for her son.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Travis Kelce Discusses 'Magical' Taylor Swift Wedding, 'So Thankful for Everybody'
articles.summary: Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce discussed his recent wedding with pop star Taylor Swift on the latest edition of the New Heights podcast, which dropped Wednesday.
articles.body:
Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce discussed his recent wedding with pop star Taylor Swift on the latest edition of the New Heights podcast, which dropped Wednesday.

During a conversation with his brother, former Philadelphia Eagles center Jason Kelce, Travis showed his appreciation for the guests and everyone who made it a special night for him and Taylor (beginning at the 11:37 mark of the podcast) .

"Me and Taylor are so thankful for everybody that showed up, from the vows to just seeing everyone, to how much fun we had, throughout the entire evening and hearing that, kind of be relayed through everybody's stories of the night," Kelce said. "And it was just so magical, man."

Kelce went on to note that he wished the wedding "could have lasted even longer than it did," because of the enjoyable time that was had by all.

The wedding took place at Madison Square Garden in New York City on July 3, and Kelce explained that he and Swift chose the unique venue because they wanted to get married "somewhere where we could have a very intimate and genuine setting without a lot of distractions."

Kelce expressed his gratitude to MSG for delivering on what they wanted, and he also gave a "special thank you" to actor Adam Sandler, who officiated the wedding.

Now, Kelce is deep in preparations for the start of his 14th NFL season, all of which have been spent in Kansas City.

An 11-time Pro Bowler, four-time First Team All-Pro and three-time Super Bowl champion, Kelce is already widely regarded as one of the greatest tight ends in NFL history and a future Pro Football Hall of Famer.

There were plenty of rumors and speculation that he would retire after the 2025 season, but he is back for at least one more campaign, as he looks to help the Chiefs get back to the playoffs after falling short last season.

articles.title: Predicting Every Game of the 2026 NFL Season: NFC South

articles.body:
If you're trying to predict an NFL team's end-of-season record, the wrong way to do it is to bring up the schedule and pick results of each game. You simply can't hope to predict stuff that well, and you'd be better served finding a method that assigns a percent chance of winning each game, adding up those percentages and converting it to a win/loss record. Going game-by-game is silly.

Because of that opening paragraph, what follows isn't betting advice . It is just a look at the schedule for each NFL team in 2026 and how things might shape up for them this season. Below, check out the 2026 week-by-week results for each NFL team with some thoughts on their outlook.

NFC South below. All odds cited are per DraftKings Sportsbook.

Game-by-Game Results for 2026: NFC South

The Falcons get off to a good start to their 2026 season.

It's 2-0 for Atlanta. First time since 2023, only the second since 2017.

Atlanta gets its first loss of the season in Green Bay.

The Saints pull the Falcons back to .500.

Remember when the Falcons said they weren't going to pursue Lamar Jackson? I bet he does.

And with this, the formerly 2-0 Falcons fall to 2-5.

Atlanta finally gets another win by beating the Bucs.

Atlanta over Kansas City in the Tony Gonzalez Bowl.

The Falcons travel to Minnesota and get a post-bye win.

Make it three straight for the Falcons and they're back to 6-6.

The Browns take down whoever is under center for Atlanta by this point.

On the road at Washington, another loss.

That's two five-game losing streaks for Atlanta in 2026, with a 6-1 record otherwise.

After a surprise playoff berth last year, Carolina starts slow in 2026.

Make it 0-2 for the defending NFC South champions.

The Panthers get on the board at Cleveland.

It's two in a row for the Panthers with a surprise win over Detroit.

After a bye, the Panthers fall in Philadelphia.

The Panthers take down the Buccaneers at home.

Once again, the Panthers surprise the Packers.

The Broncos have a tough time taking down the Panthers.

Carolina travels to New Orleans and beats the Saints.

Baltimore has an easy time taking down Carolina.

Tampa takes down Carolina, and the Panthers fall to 5-6.

Brian Flores' defense beats up on the powerless Panthers.

That's five straight losses for Carolina.

Seven straight losses for the Panthers after starting 5-4.

It's a meaningless win, but at least it's a win to close the season.

That's 0-2 for the Saints, but it's two tough matchups on the road.

Shough gets his first win of the season against the hapless Raiders.

Back to .500 with a home win over the Falcons.

The Saints got their first win of 2025 over the Giants, but they lose this time.

At least we can trust the French to more or less pronounce "Etienne" correctly, right?

Once again, the Saints are back to .500.

New Orleans takes down Carolina in a home game.

Through Week 11, the Saints will be alternating two-game winning and losing streaks.

articles.title: 5 offenses to avoid in 2026 fantasy football drafts, including Falcons
articles.summary: These offenses aren't capable of producing consistent fantasy production
articles.body:
Fantasy football is about the players you don't take as much as the players who do land on your roster. Strategically avoiding the inevitable busts each season is a reliable way to win a spot in championship week, but it's easier said than done.

Injuries, scheme or coaching changes and roster turnover can make a player who excelled one season an afterthought the next. That's why identifying fantasy-friendly teams can be a valuable exercise in the draft process.

Good teams typically have less year-over-year change, and even while a coordinator may leave for a head coaching job, organizational stability built through winning should keep things running as normal -- usually with an established quarterback in place.

Bad teams, on the other hand, are defined by chaos, usually with a new coach, quarterback -- or both -- trying to figure it out on the fly. Here are five teams that fit the bill, meaning you should avoid targeting their players in 2026 fantasy drafts.

Bijan Robinson is widely considered a top-five pick in fantasy drafts with Drake London not far behind as a fringe first-rounder. Both should be avoided at cost, as the Falcons' quarterback situation is possibly the NFL's worst with a clearly past-his-prime Tua Tagovailoa battling the oft-injured Michael Penix Jr. This offense will make you pull your hair out.

The Browns are starting Deshaun Watson after two Achilles tears, have their worst offensive line in years and play in largely awful weather for the second half of the season. Those factors are enough to fade an otherwise promising skill group consisting of tight end Harold Fannin Jr., running back Quinshon Judkins, and wide receivers KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston. Check back in on the Browns when they have an exciting young quarterback next year.

Reports out of training camp suggest Cam Ward isn't taking the second-year leap many were expecting, plus top-five pick Carnell Tate has been invisible in the preseason. With a below-average offensive line and a new coaching staff in place around them, this is an offense worth monitoring for 2027 but fading this year.

First-year coach Mike LaFleur stupefyingly gave first-round pick Jeremiyah Love 14 carries in his preseason debut, and now the star running back is battling a high ankle sprain with the season approaching. Oh, and garbage time king Jacoby Brissett, a bottom-five starting QB, held the team hostage over contract negotiations and missed much of the offseason program. This team is a complete mess that has a better chance of getting the No. 1 pick than helping you in fantasy.

The vibes surrounding Jayden Daniels have been horrendous ever since the No. 5 controversy emerged at LSU. Add in left tackle Laremy Tunsil's season-ending injury, an aging receiver group and possibly the NFL's least talented running back room, and there's not many reasons for optimism for this unit. An injury to Daniels, who was limited to seven games last year, could make every Commanders fantasy option unplayable.

articles.title: All-New 2026 College Football Week 1 QB Rankings: Where Does Arch Manning Land in Our Top 10?
articles.summary: Similar to the NFL, a gifted quarterback can turn a college football program into a playoff contender. This season’s crop […]
articles.body:
Similar to the NFL, a gifted quarterback can turn a college football program into a playoff contender. This season's crop of QB talent is filled with players who should hear their names called in Rounds 1 and 2 of the 2027 NFL Draft . But which signal callers stand above the rest as the best of the best entering the new season?

We look to answer that question with our brand new rankings of the top 10 QBs heading into Week 1 of the 2026 college football season.

There was a lot of buzz about South Carolina's Lanorris Sellers before last season because he was coming off a breakout campaign in 2024, when he tossed for 2,534 yards, ran for 674 and had 25 total TDs as a sophomore. Unfortunately, he and the Gamecocks took a disappointing step backward last year.

If South Carolina can be more like the team they were two years ago, Sellers definitely has the talent to become a household name in 2026.

Indiana head coach Curt Cignetti and his staff worked their magic with Cal transfer Fernando Mendoza last year. Turning him into the latest Heisman winner and the leader of a team that brought the school its first football national title. They are hoping to do it again in 2026, this time with former TCU star Josh Hoover.

The senior had two rock-solid seasons for the Horned Frogs in 2024 and 2025. Peaking with a career-best 29 TDs last year. However, he also had a career-high 13 INTs. If he can cut down on his mistakes, he has the talent and support around him to be an elite QB all season.

Outside of Miami landing Mensah, Lane Kiffin making Sam Leavitt his first starting QB at LSU was one of the top stories that came out of the transfer portal in the spring. Heading into the 2025 season, the former Arizona State QB was on a lot of early Heisman candidate lists. However, a Lisfranc injury limited him to just seven games last year.

Not only is Leavitt dangerous in the passing game, but he can also put the ball down and make plays with his feet. He will have even better weapons around him in Baton Rouge and can end up in the Heisman conversation again as the year progresses.

Being the starting QB for an iconic program like Notre Dame comes with a lot of pressure. The type of pressure freshmen are not usually ready for. However, CJ Carr won the QB1 job last summer and was impressive in his first year as a starter in South Bend.

The youngster posted 2,741 passing yards, with 24 TDs to 6 INTs, and a noteworthy 168.1 passer rating. While he lost a pair of great running backs to the NFL, he continues to have his name thrust into the Heisman conversation because of the expectation that 2026 will be a breakout year for Carr.

Trinidad Chambliss was one of the best stories in college football last year. The junior college star lost the QB1 battle in camp to Austin Simmons. However, Simmons suffered a serious injury in Ole Miss' Week 2 game against Kentucky . Thrusting Chambliss into the starting role for a significant amount of time. Well, he never gave Simmons a chance to get the job back.

The senior threw for nearly 4,000 yards, ran for over 500 more, and posted 30 total TDs to 3 INTs last season. His strong showing in the playoffs only added to his legend, and it likely played a role in Mississippi judicial officials granting him another year of eligibility in 2026.

Oregon QB1 Dante Moore has put himself in an interesting position. He likely would have been at least the No. 2 pick in April's NFL Draft but chose to return for another season in Eugene. That was not planned, so the Ducks added former Nebraska starter Dylan Raiola in the transfer portal. It puts unexpected pressure on the junior because a talented QB is waiting in the wings.

However, if Moore takes another step forward in 2026 like he did last year when he threw for over 3,500 yards, 30 touchdowns, and hit on 71.8 percent of his passes, he should be just fine. While the Oregon QB tailed off late last year, he is getting a lot of Heisman buzz heading into this season.

A case can be made that Texas QB Arch Manning is the most famous player in college football right now. But it's not because he was amazing in his first year as a starter in 2025. It's because he has two former NFL stars as uncles, and he was the most hyped high school player of the decade two years ago.

However, he did perform well as a sophomore last year despite sky-high expectations. Throwing for 3,163 yards, ran for 399 more, with 36 total TDs and 7 INTS. If Manning can cut down on his mistakes and be more accurate, the talent is there to be in the conversation as the best player in the nation this season.

One of the biggest signings in the transfer portal this spring was Miami replacing Carson Beck with Duke star Darian Mensah. The former Blue Devils QB had a dynamite year in his lone season at Durham as he finished second in the nation in passing yards (3,973) and touchdowns (34).

If he can put up those numbers at Duke, with even better talent around him at the U, Mensah is primed to become a household name and Heisman Trophy finalist this year.

Ohio State's Julian Sayin had big shoes to fill last season. Will Howard wasn't one of the best QBs in the country when he started for the Buckeyes in 2024. But he did something many of his predecessors didn't by helping lead OSU to a national title. Yet, despite the high expectations as the QB1 for a program looking to repeat as champs, Sayin delivered in 2025.

The first-time starter posted 3,610 yards through the air with 32 TDs and 8 INTs. He was also one of the most efficient passers in the country. Tallying a 77.0 completion percentage last year. Sayin has all the skills and the talent around him to put up big numbers again against tough competition in 2026.

When healthy, USC's Jayden Maiava is one of the most dangerous passers in the country. He showed that last season when the Trojans star posted 3,711 passing yards with 24 touchdowns to 10 interceptions.

The QB has a quick release and may be the best deep ball thrower in the nation. Maiava's biggest issue has been his riskiness with the ball. But in his 2026 debut, he showed the peaks of his talent by hitting on 25 of 29 passes for 286 yards, two touchdowns, and no interceptions against San Jose State .
